Find your way through German bureaucracy (Standesamt, documents, translations).
It's January 2034. Mara and Jakob are at the Pankow registry office to register for their marriage. The registrar, Mrs Kranz, reads out the list of documents.
Right. Mr Lorenz, your documents are complete. Mrs Ionescu, a few are still missing in your case. The Romanian birth certificate must be presented with an apostille.
With an apostille? I don't have one. Can that be done here, in Berlin?
Unfortunately not. The apostille has to be applied for in Romania. And then the certificate has to be translated into German by a sworn translator.
And how long does that take? The wedding is on the third of May.
That's hard to say. With a bit of luck it can be done in six weeks. On top of that, we need a certificate of no impediment to marriage from Romania.
A what? The word can barely be pronounced.
A certificate of no impediment to marriage. It confirms that you're not already married. It has to be applied for at the Romanian consulate.
And if it doesn't come in time? Can the date be postponed?
Anything can be postponed. But in May the appointments are almost fully booked. I'd advise you to start right away.
That's unbelievable. In Romania they say Romanian bureaucracy is the worst in the world.
Mrs Ionescu, I've been working here for thirty years. Believe me: the German one can't be beaten. But it can be solved. Almost always.

It started with a list. Mrs Kranz at the Pankow registry office had printed it out, on two pages, and Mara stuck it on the fridge at home, next to her shift plan and the photo of the proposal in Kollwitzpark. Eleven points. Nine concerned her, two concerned Jakob. Jakob's two points were dealt with in a week: his ID card, and his birth certificate from the registry office in his village in Thuringia, which had sent it to him two days after his phone call, with a handwritten greeting from the registrar who had known him as a little boy with a cello. Mara's nine points were another story.

Mrs Kranz herself was a woman who frightened Mara at first. She was small, grey-haired, with rimless glasses and a voice that never got louder or quieter, whatever you told her. On her desk there was no photo, no plant, just a rotating rack with twelve stamps, lined up next to each other like soldiers. Jakob whispered on the way out: “I don't think she's smiled once in thirty years.” Mara didn't answer. She had seen that on the wall behind Mrs Kranz there hung, very small, a child's drawing: a house, a sun and underneath, in crooked handwriting: “For Grandma Gisela, the wedding lady.”

The birth certificate was the first problem. Mara had one, of course, but it was an old one, from 1999, on thin paper, with a stamp so faded that it could barely be read any more. “It can't be presented like that,” Mrs Kranz had said, kindly but firmly. “You need a new copy issued, an apostille and a certified translation. In that order.” Mara rang her mother in Sibiu. Elena went to the town hall the next morning, waited two hours in a corridor with green walls and came back with the news that the new certificate could be collected in ten days. The apostille then had to be applied for at the court. That would take another two weeks.

Then came the certificate of no impediment to marriage, a word Mara couldn't pronounce for three days without laughing. It had to be applied for at the Romanian consulate in Berlin, in person, with an appointment. The next free appointment was in seven weeks. Mara sat at the kitchen table in front of her laptop and stared at the calendar. Seven weeks. Then the translation. Then the registration. The wedding was on the third of May. It couldn't be done. For the first time since she had come to Berlin, she put her head on the table and cried with rage because of a form.

Jakob found her like that when he came home from school. He sat down next to her, said nothing and made tea. Then he took the list off the fridge and read it once more, point by point, slowly, the way he read his pupils' essays. And then he said something that Mara later described as the moment she knew she was marrying the right man: “Do you know who lives in this house? Someone who worked for a German public authority for forty years. And someone whose wife wrote over a hundred petitions to the GDR authorities. And won most of them.”
Fritz, who was with them that afternoon because Ludwig was at the doctor's, laid his grey head in her lap and sighed, as if he understood everything.

Ludwig listened to it all that evening, in Ingrid's armchair, with the list on his knee and the magnifying glass in his hand. He read every point twice. Then he took an old folder out of the cupboard in the hall, on which was written in Ingrid's handwriting: “Authorities. What can be solved.” Inside were thirty years of letters, applications, complaints and replies, carefully sorted. Right at the front, on a separate sheet, Ingrid had noted down three rules. “One: every problem can be solved if you find the right person. Two: the right person never sits at the first counter. Three: always be polite. But never give up.”

While Mara read the rules, Ludwig told her how in 1987 Ingrid had managed, with great difficulty, to get a flat for a family with five children who had been living for three years in two rooms without a bathroom. She had written seven petitions. She had been to the housing office four times. The fifth time she didn't wait at the counter, but walked straight into the head of department's office, with a cake and with the five children, all nicely combed and in their best clothes. “The man played with the children for half an hour,” said Ludwig. “Then he signed the allocation. Ingrid said: you can refuse a person a form. But you can't refuse a child a home.”

The next morning Ludwig rang the Romanian consulate. First he spoke to a woman on the phone who told him that appointments could only be made online. Then to a man who told him that unfortunately the waiting time could not be shortened. Then, after half an hour and three transfers, to an older consulate official, Mrs Popa, who happened to be from Sibiu and happened to have grown up on the same street as Elena Ionescu. Ludwig told her the whole story, about the nurse with the suitcase, about the choir, about the cello, about the song from Thuringia. Mrs Popa listened. Then she said: “Bring the young woman to me on Thursday at eight. Before opening time. It can be done.”
He had put on a shirt specially for it, even though nobody could see him on the phone. “Authorities can sense that,” he told Fritz, who looked at him without understanding.

In Sibiu, meanwhile, Dan did something nobody would have expected of him. The quiet beekeeper, who never said much and feared authorities more than a swarm of bees, put on his only suit, took a large jar of honey under his arm and went to the court to apply for the apostille. At the counter sat a young man who explained to him that the processing time was unfortunately fourteen days. Dan said nothing. He just put the jar of honey on the counter, very slowly, and told him in three sentences that his daughter wanted to marry a teacher who played the cello in Berlin and that the wedding was on the third of May. The young man looked at the jar, then at Dan, then at the jar again. “Come on Friday,” he said. And then, more quietly: “My grandmother kept bees too.”

The certificate with the apostille arrived in Berlin by courier twelve days later, together with a little jar of honey for Ludwig, “from a grateful beekeeper”. Andrei knew a sworn translator, an elderly gentleman from Timișoara who had lived in Kreuzberg for fifty years and did the translation in one day, at half price, because, as he said, “he hadn't translated a marriage document in years, only divorces”. And on Thursday at eight, before opening time, Mara was at the Romanian consulate with Mrs Popa, who offered her coffee, showed her photos of her grandchildren and after twenty minutes handed her the certificate of no impediment to marriage, with a stamp so fresh that the ink was still shining.

Outside, in front of the consulate, Mara immediately rang her mother. Elena cried on the phone, then laughed, then told her that Mrs Popa was the daughter of the woman who, when Elena was a child in Sibiu, had the little corner shop that sold the best croissants in the Lower Town. “You see,” said Elena, “the world is a village. And Sibiu is the middle of it.” Mara laughed and looked up at the sky above the consulate, where a little Romanian flag was fluttering in the wind, and thought that Ingrid's first rule was true. You just had to find the right person. And sometimes the right person found you.

When Mara and Jakob stood in front of Mrs Kranz again three weeks later with all the documents, the registrar leafed through everything, page by page, stamp by stamp, with a frown. Then she put the folder down and looked at the two of them over her glasses. “Mrs Ionescu,” she said, “I've been working here for thirty years. I've never seen anyone get through this list in six weeks. With an apostille from Romania. How did you do it?” Mara looked at Jakob, then smiled. “With an old tram driver,” she said, “a jar of honey and a woman who has been dead for twelve years and still solves all the problems.”

Mrs Kranz laughed, for the first time since Mara had known her, and stamped the marriage registration, with a strong, firm blow. “The third of May, eleven o'clock,” she said. “And tell the old tram driver: if he's ever looking for work, he can start with me.” That evening, Mara stuck the list back on the fridge, with eleven green ticks. Underneath she stuck Ingrid's three rules, which Ludwig had copied out for her. They're still there today.

And on the wall of the Pankow registry office, behind Mrs Kranz's desk, next to her granddaughter's drawing, from the following week there hung something else: a little jar of honey from Sibiu, with a note written by Mara: “For the wedding lady. Thank you for not giving up.” Jakob, who saw it at the wedding in May, admitted later that he had been wrong. Mrs Kranz could smile. She just didn't do it often. And when she did, she did it with all her heart.
